name: Trolamine salicylate

lead: Trolamine salicylate is a salicylate salt best known as the active ingredient in over-the-counter topical pain creams. It has also been used as a weak UVB filter in sunscreens and cosmetics, which is its minor link to skin protection.

The salicylate part absorbs UVB, and triethanolamine neutralises the acid. In 2019 the US FDA proposed that its sunscreen use is not generally recognised as safe and effective. Small trials from the 1980s and 1990s studied it for knee osteoarthritis and exercise-induced soreness, with mixed results.

paras: People mostly use it as an odourless rub for aches in muscles and joints. As a sunscreen ingredient it appeared in older formulas as a supporting filter.
Labels say external use only. Listed hazards include eye damage and skin or eye irritation. Absorbed salicylate has been measured in blood after topical use in a small human study.

chain: Mild sun-filter role in old products
angle.text: Trolamine salicylate is best known as the active in odourless muscle-pain creams, and was historically used as a weak UVB absorber in sunscreens and cosmetics. Its link to appearance is minor: the salicylate absorbs some UVB, which gave it an occasional supporting role in older sun products.

lead: Trolamine salicylate (triethanolamine salicylate) is a salt of triethanolamine and salicylic acid used in over-the-counter topical pain-relief creams such as Aspercreme, and historically as a weak UVB absorber in sunscreens and cosmetics.[1] The salicylate absorbs UVB, the triethanolamine neutralises acidity, and the compound is odourless, unlike menthol-based rubs.[1]

Products are marketed for temporary relief of minor aches in muscles and joints from arthritis, backache, strains and sprains.[1][2] In 2019 the US FDA proposed classifying its use in sunscreens as not generally recognised as safe and effective.[1] Small trials from the 1980s and 1990s examined its effect on knee osteoarthritis and exercise-induced soreness, with mixed results across studies.

paras: Topical analgesic: US label wording for a trolamine salicylate product states it is for temporary relief of minor aches and pains of muscles and joints associated with arthritis, simple backache, lumbago, neuralgia, strains, bruises and sprains, for external use only.[2] Wikipedia notes listed products are 10% solutions.[1]
Sunscreen and cosmetics: it has served as a weak UVB filter, though Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, says this use has been discontinued.[3]

As a salicylate it is described as inhibiting cyclo-oxygenase enzymes and so reducing prostaglandin production locally.[3] A 1984 pig study found that at least 82% of an applied dose was absorbed over two hours, with salicylate localising in underlying muscle.[4] A 1996 human crossover study compared serum salicylate after topical methyl salicylate and trolamine salicylate application.[5]
Wikipedia states that the FDA has not reviewed the listed OTC products and that manufacturers have not given the agency evidence of absorption into underlying tissue.[1]

Wikipedia lists a GHS warning for serious eye damage, skin and eye irritation, and harm if swallowed.[1] Labels advise external use only, and Grokipedia says use should be avoided on broken skin and under occlusive dressings.[2][3]

A 1982 JAMA report examined a trolamine salicylate cream in knee osteoarthritis, and a 1998 study examined a single topical application in osteoarthritis symptoms.[6][7] Studies of delayed-onset muscle soreness include a 1991 trial of ultrasound with trolamine salicylate phonophoresis in 40 young women and a 1989 trial of a 10% cream after weight training.[8][9] A 1988 conference abstract cited by Wikipedia reported less soreness with the product than placebo.[1] A 1999 rat study compared topical agents including trolamine salicylate for failing skin flaps.[10] No clinical trials of its sunscreen performance were found.

timeline.event: US FDA proposes that trolamine salicylate in sunscreens is not generally recognised as safe and effective.[1]
